about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

references: Turcotte, D. L. and Schubert, G. 2014, Geodynamics, 3rd edn, Cambridge University Press, section 2.2. doi:10.1017/CBO9780511843877

equation.name: Pressure from the weight of a layer

source.text: Turcotte, D. L. and Schubert, G. 2014, Geodynamics, 3rd edn, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: The deeper you go, the more weight sits on top of you. Ten kilometres of water presses about a thousand times harder than the air.
explain.science: Pressure added by a layer of constant density under constant gravity. Fine for oceans and crusts much thinner than the radius; deep interiors need gravity that falls with depth.

references: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127: mass-radius relation for rocky planets based on PREM, eq. 2 (inverse eq. 3). doi:10.3847/0004-637X/819/2/127

equation.name: Size of a rocky world from its mass and core

f.name: share of the mass in the core

c0.name: radius at no core, Earth radii per Earth mass^(1/3.7)

source.text: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127

explain.curious: An iron-rich rocky world is smaller than a rock-rich one of the same mass, because iron packs tighter.
explain.science: Fit to two-layer (iron core, silicate mantle) models scaled from Earth's seismic profile (PREM), for rocky planets without water or atmosphere. Agrees with the model curves to about 0.01 R⊕ in its range (1 to 8 M⊕, core mass fraction 0 to 0.4); the inverse gives core mass fraction to about ±0.02.

references: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127: mass-radius relation for rocky planets based on PREM, eq. 2 (inverse eq. 3). doi:10.3847/0004-637X/819/2/127

equation.name: Share of a rocky world's mass in its core
equation.formula:
x = M / M_e
r = R / R_e
f = (c0 - r / x ^ (1 / c2)) / c1

c0.name: radius at no core, Earth radii per Earth mass^(1/3.7)

f.name: share of the mass in the core

source.text: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127

explain.curious: Weigh a rocky world and measure it, and you can tell roughly how much of it is an iron core.
explain.science: The Zeng et al. 2016 relation inverted. Outside 0 to 0.4 the answer means the world is not a dry iron and rock planet (too fluffy: water or gas; too dense: more iron than the fit covers).

references: Zeng, L. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2017, ApJ 837, 164: a simple analytical model for rocky planet interiors (core radius fraction about the square root of core mass fraction). doi:10.3847/1538-4357/aa6218

equation.name: Size of a rocky world's core

f.name: share of the mass in the core

source.text: Zeng, L. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2017, ApJ 837, 164

explain.curious: How far down you would dig before reaching the iron core.
explain.science: For rocky planets the core radius fraction is close to the square root of the core mass fraction (Earth: 0.57 predicted, 0.55 measured).
